prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Other weddings are so shrewd on the sofa, short and baffled, bassett-legged. All things knuckled, I have no winter left, in my sore rememory, to melt down for drinking water. Shrunk down. Your wedding slides the way wiry dark hairs do, down a swimming pool drain. So I am drained. Sincerely. I wish you every chapped bird on this pilgrimage to hold your hem up from the dust. Dust is plural: infinite dust. I will sink in the sun, I will crawl towards the heavy drawing and design the curtains in the room of never marrying you. Because it is a sinking, because today’s perfect weather is a later life’s smut. This soiled future unplans love. I keep unplanning the same Sunday. Leg and flower, breeze and terrier, I have no garden and couldn’t be happier. Please, don’t lose me here. I am sorry my clutch is all tendon and no discipline: the heart is a severed kind of muscle and alone. I can hear yours in your room. I hear mine in another room. In another’s.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker feels emotionally drained and diminished by the thought of another person’s wedding.
- The speaker mourns a lost or impossible love that they imagine as a future of never marrying the beloved.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Other, All, Shrunk

outputs.L1: Other weddings sit so shrewdly on the sofa: short and baffled, basset-legged. All things knuckled, I have no winter left, in my sore rememory, to melt down for drinking water. Shrunk down. Your wedding slips the way wiry dark hairs do, down a swimming pool drain. And so I am drained. Sincerely. I wish you every chapped bird on this pilgrimage to hold your hem above the dust. Dust is plural: infinite dust. I will sink in the sun; I will crawl toward the heavy drawing and design the curtains in the room of never marrying you. Because it is a sinking, because today’s perfect weather is a later life’s smut. This soiled future unplans love. I keep unplanning the same Sunday. Leg and flower, breeze and terrier: I have no garden and could not be happier. Please, don’t lose me here. I am sorry my clutch is all tendon and no discipline; the heart is a severed kind of muscle, and alone. I can hear yours in your room. I hear mine in another room. In another’s.
outputs.L2:
Other ceremonies perch cunningly on the couch—brief, bewildered, low to the ground like basset hounds. Everything is bent at the knuckles. In my aching memory, there is no winter remaining that I can thaw into water to drink. Everything has dwindled.

Your wedding slips away like thin black hairs spiraling into the drain of a swimming pool. And so I am emptied. Truly. I hope every raw, wind-cracked bird along this journey lifts your hem clear of the dirt. Dirt multiplies; dust is endless.

I will go down beneath the sun. I will drag myself toward the dense sketch, then make the curtains for the chamber where I never become your spouse. For this is a descent, and the flawless weather of this day will become the grime of some later existence. That stained future erases love before it can happen. I keep erasing that same Sunday before it arrives.

Limb and blossom, wind and small dog: I own no garden, and I am gladder than I should be. Please do not let me disappear in this place. Forgive me—my grip is nothing but sinew, without control. The heart is a muscle cut loose, solitary by nature. I can hear yours beating in your room. I hear my own from a different room. From someone else’s.
outputs.L3:
The speaker is emotionally overwhelmed by the thought of another person’s wedding. Rather than experiencing the occasion as joyful, they feel drained, diminished, and almost emptied by it. The wedding becomes a reminder of what they themselves have lost or can never have, intensifying their sense of sorrow and exclusion.

At the centre of the poem is a mourning for a lost or impossible love. The speaker imagines a future defined not by union, but by the painful certainty of never marrying the beloved. This imagined future turns love into something marked by absence, longing, and denial. Marriage, which might usually symbolize fulfilment, instead becomes a symbol of what is permanently out of reach.

The poem presents love as painful, unstable, and repeatedly undone. Rather than offering comfort or security, love appears fragile and vulnerable to separation, regret, and emotional collapse. The speaker’s feelings seem to be constantly broken apart and reassembled, suggesting that love is not a settled state but an ongoing source of disturbance.

There is also a strong sense of regret and vulnerability in the speaker’s voice. The heart is described as isolated and wounded, emphasizing the depth of their emotional suffering. This image suggests not only heartbreak, but also loneliness: the speaker’s pain is private, enclosed, and difficult to share.

Finally, the speaker feels profoundly separated from the beloved. Even when they imagine a connection between their hearts, that connection is distorted by distance. It is as if the two hearts are beating in different rooms, or even in entirely different lives. This separation reinforces the poem’s central sadness: love exists, but it cannot bring the speaker and the beloved together.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a speaker who is caught in the emotional aftermath of love, watching or imagining another person’s wedding from a position of grief, jealousy, and exclusion. Rather than describing the event in a straightforward way, it moves through surreal and fragmented images that mirror the speaker’s inner disorientation. The wedding becomes more than a social ceremony: it is a symbol of a future that has continued without the speaker, a future in which someone else has been chosen and the speaker has been left behind.

Throughout the piece, the speaker’s voice feels intimate and confessional, as if they are trying to admit feelings that are painful, shameful, or difficult to organize. Jealousy appears not only as resentment toward the wedding itself, but also as a deeper sorrow over the loss of possibility. The speaker is not simply mourning a person; they are mourning the life they imagined with that person. This gives the text its sense of alienation. The speaker exists outside the celebration, outside the couple’s happiness, and outside the future they once hoped would include them.

The phrase “unplanned” suggests that the speaker has been forced into a life they did not choose. Their future has arrived by accident, shaped by separation rather than intention. In this way, the text becomes a meditation on love’s aftermath: what remains after desire has failed, after intimacy has ended, and after another person’s commitment makes that ending undeniable. The surreal imagery reflects the instability of grief, while the fragmented structure captures the way heartbreak interrupts ordinary thought. Ultimately, the text portrays the loneliness of not being chosen and the painful realization that love can continue to matter even after it has nowhere left to go.
outputs.L5:
**Other, All, Shrunk**

In a world that once felt endless, everything had somehow shrunk. The cities seemed smaller, the distances shorter, and even dreams appeared to fit inside the tiny screens people carried in their hands. All that was once grand and mysterious had become measured, labeled, and stored away.

Yet there was always the other side—the part that could not be reduced. Other thoughts, other possibilities, other paths remained hidden beyond the ordinary. While all things around us may seem to have shrunk, imagination still refuses to become small. It stretches beyond limits, reminding us that even in a narrowed world, there is always room for wonder.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem addressed to an ex-lover on their wedding day, full of strange bodily imagery, grief, weather, dust, and the feeling of never marrying them.
counterfactuals.output:
Beloved who is no longer mine,

today the sky wears rice in its hair. The church bells cough doves into the weather, and every cloud has a mouth full of white thread. Somewhere, you are lifting your hands into the sleeves of a future I was never allowed to touch. Somewhere, another person is fastening the small bright hooks of the world around you.

I woke with dust on my tongue, as if the house had been grinding its teeth all night. The mirror showed me my face, but only reluctantly: a wet map, a country after evacuation. My ribs opened and closed like umbrellas in a storm that had forgotten the meaning of rain. In the basin, my heart floated face-down, a red fruit bruised by its own ripening.

Do you remember the summer we almost became inevitable? The air was heavy with insects and prophecy. We slept like two knives in the same drawer. You put your ear to my chest and said you heard horses. I said they were coming for us. I was wrong. They were only passing through.

Now the weather has married you before I could. It leans over your veil and kisses the back of your neck with its damp gray lips. The wind, that old gossip, carries your name through alleys and under doors, lays it in the corners where dust gathers into little parliaments. Every mote votes against me. Every mote says: not yours, not yours, not yours.

I imagine your body today as a house lit from within: wrists like windows, throat like a staircase, mouth a room where vows are laid out clean and warm. I imagine another hand entering that house without knocking. I imagine your new life growing organs—golden lungs, silver stomach, a spine of bells. I imagine it swallowing you kindly.

And I stand outside with my pockets full of unsent winters.

There is a grief that does not wail but molts. It leaves skins everywhere: in drawers, in shoes, in the sugar bowl. I find pieces of myself in impossible places—the small intestine of a glove, the eyelid of a spoon, the kneecap of an afternoon. I have become a museum of what did not happen. Here is the dress I never wore beside you. Here is the ring-shaped absence. Here is the bed, preserved in dust, where our possible children sleep as quietly as fossils.

The rain begins, though the forecast promised mercy. It taps the roof with a thousand fingernails, asking to be let in. I let it. I let everything in today: the weather, the mildew, the blue ache, the choir of dead plans humming in the walls. My hands fill with mud. My mouth fills with birds. My shadow lies down and refuses to continue.

You are marrying someone else.

The sentence is simple. It has no antlers, no blood, no wings. Yet it walks through me like an animal made of glass, cutting everything luminous as it goes.

I hope they love you in the mornings when your soul is still unbuttoned. I hope they learn the weather of your silences, the soft avalanches behind your eyes. I hope they know that sometimes your laughter breaks open and a child climbs out, barefoot and astonished. I hope they do not fear the dark orchard in your chest, or the bees that sleep there.

As for me, I will keep not marrying you.

I will do it faithfully. I will wake and not marry you. I will drink coffee and not marry you. I will grow older in rooms that never held our vows, beneath ceilings powdered with dust, beneath weather that forgets your face and then remembers it all at once. I will carry the phantom weight of your hand at the end of my arm. I will walk down no aisle toward you forever.

Today, while flowers rot beautifully in vases and the guests lift their glasses like small, transparent throats, I send you this: a storm folded into an envelope, a lungful of dust, a blessing with its bones showing.

May your joy be real.

May my grief learn to become weather.

May the life we never lived lie down gently beside me, at last, and sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental literary monologue in the style of contemporary prose poetry: bitter, tender, and uncanny, about attending someone else’s wedding while still being in love with them.
counterfactuals.output:
I wore the dress you never saw me in, which made it faithful.

All afternoon the church kept breathing through its stained-glass lungs, blue then red then butcher-gold across the pews, across the shoulders of your relatives, across the bride’s white spine like a hand deciding not to touch. I sat four rows back, beside an aunt who smelled of lilacs and old smoke, and I folded my hands until they looked borrowed.

You were beautiful in the usual unbearable way: hair combed, throat shaved, face arranged into the public version of happiness. I knew the private drafts. I knew the sleep-stung face, the cruel laugh at midnight, the way you said my name once into the hollow of my wrist as if testing whether it might echo. It did. It still does. That is the embarrassing part. That is the little animal I smuggled in under my ribs.

When she came down the aisle, everyone stood. I stood too. I am not a monster, or I am a well-trained one. Her veil moved like weather. She was lovely. She was not me, which is not a crime, though I treated it as evidence.

The priest spoke of union. Of patience. Of the mystery of two becoming one, as if arithmetic had not always been the first violence. I watched your mouth form vows. Your voice did not break. Mine did, quietly, somewhere no one could hear it: a glass dropped in another room, a bird striking the black window of the heart.

At the reception, the chandeliers hung above us like rich jellyfish. Champagne rose in flutes, all those pale trapped bubbles hurrying upward to disappear. I ate the salmon. I complimented the flowers. I let strangers mistake me for strong.

Your mother kissed my cheek and said, “I’m so glad you came,” and I almost answered, I came because grief has manners. I came because love is sometimes a taxidermied thing you carry to the party and prop in a chair. I came because I wanted to see if the world would end politely.

It didn’t.

The band played something with trumpets. Children slid under tables in their patent shoes. Someone’s grandfather wept openly into a napkin, spared by age from having to disguise the obvious. I watched you dance with her, your hand at her back, steering her gently through the bright aquarium of the room. You used to dance badly with me in kitchens. No music, just the refrigerator humming its idiot hymn, your socks slipping, my face in your shoulder, the future standing outside the window with its mouth full of snow.

Once, near the bar, you touched my elbow.

Just that.

A small courtesy. A spark from a dead wire.

“You okay?” you asked, and the tenderness in it was indecent. I wanted to say no. I wanted to say I have been living in the attic of that question for years. I wanted to say your happiness has teeth and it is eating through the walls. Instead I smiled, the kind of smile women learn to make from salt.

“Of course,” I said.

Of course: the saddest spell. Of course: the coffin with a ribbon on it.

You nodded, relieved. That wounded me most, your relief. How quickly mercy becomes abandonment when given by the beloved.

Later they cut the cake. Two knives, four hands, applause. The frosting was too sweet. I ate every bite as punishment or sacrament, I couldn’t tell. In my mouth, sugar turned to plaster. Around me people cheered for the clean mythology: first dance, first kiss, first slice, first night. As if love begins where witnesses can see it. As if we had not already lived an invisible country and burned its flag ourselves.

I caught the bouquet by accident.

Can you believe that? The thing flew at me like a minor curse. White roses, eucalyptus, ribbon damp from her palm. Everyone laughed. Someone shouted, “You’re next!” and I held the flowers as if they were a diagnosis. For one second I imagined walking over and placing them at your feet. Not as accusation. As offering. As proof that even ruined things can be ceremonial.

But I didn’t. I carried them to the bathroom and locked myself in a stall, where the tiles shone with a hospital sincerity. I pressed my face into the bouquet and inhaled until the roses became monstrous, until their scent was a room I could not leave. In the mirror, when I finally looked, my lipstick had faded in the center, giving me the appearance of someone half-erased by kissing.

There are humiliations no one sees. They are the ones that bloom longest.

When I left, the night was wet and black, the parking lot stippled with rain. Through the windows, the party pulsed on, golden and distant, like a ship sinking in reverse. I stood there with my useless flowers, listening to the muffled music, and I understood that I had survived. Not healed. Not risen. Just continued, which is sometimes the ugliest miracle.

A car passed, dragging light over my legs. The bouquet trembled in my hand. For a moment, I thought it was alive. For a moment, I thought everything I had lost was only hiding, crouched beneath the hedges, waiting for me to call it by its true name.

I did not call.

I walked home in the rain, carrying someone else’s future against my chest.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, dreamlike paragraph that begins with “Other weddings…” and explores heartbreak, memory, gardens, rooms, and the impossibility of marriage.
counterfactuals.output: Other weddings drifted past the windows like white moths, carrying with them the scent of bruised lilies, rain-soaked veils, and all the promises no one had the strength to keep; in every room I entered there was another room folding inside it, a bed made for absence, a mirror silvered with old departures, a chair where memory sat with its hands in its lap, while beyond the house the garden kept rehearsing its green catastrophe—roses opening like wounds, ivy spelling forgotten names on the walls, pear trees dropping their small hard hearts into the grass. I thought love would become a door, but it became a corridor; I thought grief would end, but it learned my voice and answered from the pantry, the stairwell, the locked blue chamber where your laughter was stored among cracked cups and winter coats. How could anyone marry beneath such weather, with the dead rinsing their faces in the fountains, with childhood buried under the marigolds, with every vow already echoing as an elegy? The ring was only another moon, cold and repetitive, and the bride—whoever she was, whoever I had been—stood at the threshold of an orchard in flames, holding a bouquet of keys that opened nothing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a melancholy avant-garde wedding toast from someone who was not chosen, using fragmented syntax, surreal metaphors, and emotionally raw language.
counterfactuals.output:
To the two of you—

May the glasses tremble honestly.

I stand here with my smile pinned on crooked.  
A small white flag.  
A moth in borrowed light.

You chose each other. Of course you did.  
The room knew before I did.  
The flowers knew, opening their soft mouths.  
Even the knives on the table shone like they had been warned.

And I—  
I was the door left half-open.  
The rain practicing my name.  
The extra chair in the dream where no one sits.

But love is not a courtroom.  
No verdict. No appeal.  
Just the heart, ridiculous animal,  
dragging its bright wound through the music.

So let me say this:  
you are beautiful together.  
Painfully.  
Like a cathedral made of salt before the tide comes in.  
Like two matches deciding to become one fire  
and not apologizing for the ash.

I wanted—  
No.  
This is not the place to dig up the moon and accuse it.

Tonight is yours.

May your life be full of ordinary miracles:  
coffee cooling beside shared silence,  
laundry warm as forgiveness,  
the small mercy of being seen  
and not turned away from.

May you fight clean.  
May you return.  
May you learn the terrible art  
of staying.

And if sorrow comes—because it will, dressed beautifully—  
may it find you holding hands under the table.  
May it find no empty place between you.

I raise my glass.

To the chosen.  
To the choosing.  
To the love that did not choose me  
and still taught me how enormous  
a heart can become  
while breaking.

Cheers.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic breakup letter to a person getting married to someone else; make it bizarre, intimate, and image-heavy, with phrases about dust, swimming pool drains, curtains, and hearts in separate rooms.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear You,

Today you step toward a door I am not standing behind.

I imagine the church—or the courthouse, or the garden, wherever it is—filling with light the color of old lemons, the guests arranged like careful furniture, their shoes whispering dust into the carpet. Somewhere your new beloved is fastening a cuff, smoothing a veil, becoming the room you will enter.

I am not angry. Anger is too clean for this.

What I feel is stranger: like finding my name written in mildew around the mouth of a swimming pool drain. Like waking to discover the curtains breathing in and out by themselves, keeping secrets with the window. Like our old laughter has become a small animal trapped in the walls, scratching only when it rains.

You once touched my face as if checking whether the moon was real. I kept that touch. I hid it badly. It glowed through drawers, under plates, inside the sleeves of winter coats. Even now, it follows me from room to room, wearing your hands.

But love, yours and mine, has become a house where the hearts sleep in separate rooms. Mine under a ceiling of cracked blue paint. Yours somewhere warm, with new sheets, new vows, a lamp left on for someone else.

So I am writing to let the strange little ghosts go.

Let the dust have the photographs.
Let the swimming pool drain swallow the summers.
Let the curtains close their long eyelids.
Let the rooms remain rooms.

I hope your marriage is gentle in the mornings. I hope the person waiting for you knows the tiny weather of your silence, the way you vanish when you are sad, the way joy makes you almost foolish. I hope they love you not like a prize, not like a wound, but like bread: daily, necessary, warm.

As for me, I will become unrecognizable. I will grow new shadows. I will teach my heart to sleep without listening for your footsteps in the hall.

Goodbye, beloved almost.

May your life be bright enough that even the dust forgives you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
